newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Italy wants action on Albania in U.N. Council.
newsitem.headline: Italy wants action on Albania in U.N. Council.

text.p: Italy has asked the U.N. Security Council to authorise a European-dominated force for Albania to guard deliveries of food and other necessities and help the country recover from violence and near-anarchy.
Security Council members met informally late on Thursday on the Italian request and may do so again on Friday.
Several said most delegations were in favour of endorsing a multinational force in principle but hesitated on giving quick approval without details on its mandate, its duration and who would pay.
"There has to be greater clarity all around," said one key council member, adding that the 15-member body also needed a formal request from Albania, expected to be submitted shortly.
Italy, which is expected to lead such an operation, asked the council to endorse a force urgently and meet during the three-day holiday weekend when the U.N. is officially closed.

Its ambassador, Paolo Fulci, circulated proposals for a draft resolution called for council authorisation of a force to "achieve humanitarian and other objectives" with a need to "ensure the security and freedom of movement."

The Italian proposal follows a Vienna meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which agreed to establish a mission for the purpose of "providing advice and assistance" in democratization, the media, human rights and the preparing for and monitoring Albanian elections, expected in June.

But the 54-nation body, reflecting divisions among its members, stopped short of authorising outright a police force or troops, saying the U.N. Security Council needed to give the mission a green light.
Seven Council members belong to the OSCE -- France, Britain, Russia and the United States, which are permanent members with veto power, as well as Portual and Poland.
Among those which have expressed willingness to send troops are France, Portugal, Spain and Greece, Turkey, Romania and Austria in addition to Italy.

Italy has estimated about 2,500 personnel would be deployed initially, with another 2,500 in reserve. Albania wants foreign police or troops to help secure ports, airports, roads and railroads to ensure distribution of relief supplies.

If authorised, diplomats said its status would be similar to the U.S.-led operation to expel Iraqi troops from Kuwait or France's 1994 intervention. In both cases the United Nations gave the operations international legitimacy without organising the missions.

Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular savings schemes collapsed, erasing millions of dollars. Rebels seized the south in March in an armed insurrection, blaming President Sali Berisha for the fiasco and demanding that he quit.

Since then gangs have roamed the south, stealing, looting and killing and creating a food crisis. On Thursday, 17 people died in a gun battle in Levan in central Albania in the country's most violent incident in the last two months.
On Monday, Italy decided to turn away boats bringing Albanians to its ports from across the Adriatic.
Italian military and Interior Ministry sources said the government issued its directive after nearly 12,000 Albanians arrived at southeast Italian ports in a flotilla of rusting and ancient boats.

Interior Ministry undersecretary Giannicola Sinisi told reporters that recent arrivals were "men and women from areas which have not even been touched by the revolt. They are looking for a better life, better-paid work. In short, they are immigrants. I can understand it but we cannot accept them."
